clinicalPearls: VHF is an acute viral syndrome of severe disease and multisystem organ dysfunction sharing a common disruption of vascular function, stability, and integrity; overt hemorrhage is often NOT the most prominent or severe feature, so absence of bleeding does not exclude VHF (p.1674).

Travel to an endemic or active-outbreak area within the incubation period is a major diagnostic clue; rural exposures more often suggest VHF except for urban-host/vector agents (Seoul virus, dengue, yellow fever) (p.1675).

For filovirid (Ebola/Marburg) disease, the incubation period is 2-25 days (most commonly 7-10 days), beginning with a nonspecific influenza-like illness (sudden fever/chills, headache, myalgia, pharyngitis, arthralgia, maculopapular rash) before a second phase (~5-7 days on) with GI, respiratory, cardiovascular, and CNS involvement (p.1685).

Common filovirid hemorrhagic signs are subconjunctival injection, petechial rash, gingival bleeding, and bleeding at injection sites; frank epistaxis, hematemesis, hematuria, and melena occur but are LESS common, and severe blood loss is rare (except during/after childbirth) (pp.1684-1685).
Ebola/Marburg present with very similar clinical phenotypes that cannot be distinguished at the bedside and, for practical purposes, may be managed as the same disease (p.1685).
Early recognition is crucial: prompt isolation and hospitalization are indicated even in the absence of clinical signs, with rapid triage and ongoing vital-sign monitoring (p.1675).

Filovirids are highly infectious but not exceptionally contagious; human-to-human spread occurs by direct contact with an infected person or their body fluids/tissues, with NO evidence of aerosol or respiratory droplet transmission in natural outbreak settings (p.1679).

Persistence of filovirids in immune-privileged sites (most commonly semen of male survivors; rarely CNS, eye, placenta) can cause recrudescent disease and rare reignition of outbreaks; sexual abstinence or condom use is advised for male survivors until semen is shown to be filovirid-RNA free (pp.1686-1687).
harrison.pathophysiology: Across VHFs, direct or indirect microvascular damage increases vascular permeability and (when platelet function is reduced) causes disruption and local hemorrhage, most evident in skin and mucous membranes; hypotension and shock reflect generalized circulatory dysfunction rather than life-threatening blood loss. Pathogenesis is incompletely understood and varies by virus, with direct vascular/parenchymal damage in some and soluble mediators dominating in others. For filovirids specifically, virions enter via skin lesions, mucosal surfaces, or parenteral inoculation; GP1,2 spikes engage cell-surface molecules and the intracellular receptor NPC1. First targets are macrophages, monocytes, and dendritic cells, and viral proteins (VP35, VP40, VP24) suppress innate immunity (e.g., type I interferon pathways), enabling high viral titers and widespread tissue dissemination. Hallmarks include profound immune dysregulation, massive lymphoid depletion with severe lymphopenia, coagulopathy (thrombocytopenia, elevated tissue factor, consumption of clotting factors, raised D-dimers, falling protein C; possible DIC, though controversial), hepatocyte necrosis with synthetic dysfunction contributing to coagulopathy, and endothelial dysfunction with increased vascular permeability leading to fluid redistribution, interstitial edema, and hypovolemic or septic shock (pp.1674-1675, 1683-1685).
additionalDifferentials: Falciparum malaria (a most important mimic and a treatable, potentially fatal alternative)
Other treatable travel-associated febrile illnesses: shigellosis, leptospirosis, relapsing fever, rickettsial diseases
Other VHFs/high-consequence viral infections, in particular Lassa fever and yellow fever
Dengue and other viral hemorrhagic fevers in the bleeding/febrile traveler
infectionMimics: Other high-consequence viral infections (Lassa fever, yellow fever)
nonInfectiousMimics: Acquired or inherited coagulopathies in the bleeding patient
additionalInvestigations: RT-PCR targeting one or more filovirid genes is the diagnostic assay of choice; in-field PCR platforms (e.g., Cepheid GeneXpert) are deployed during outbreaks
Acute-phase blood/serum is the preferred specimen as it usually contains high virion titers
Antigen-capture ELISA / immunochromatographic rapid diagnostic tests (currently limited; EBOV antigen RDT sensitivity restricts use largely to postmortem samples)
IgM- and IgG-capture ELISAs (including multiplex) for antibodies in later disease and in survivors
Virus isolation/plaque assays and electron microscopy require maximum-containment laboratories; in-field genome sequencing supports outbreak epidemiology

Supportive labs typically show leukopenia (then leukocytosis), thrombocytopenia, raised aminotransferases (AST > ALT) and GGT, raised creatinine/urea with proteinuria, electrolyte derangement, hypoglycemia, hypoalbuminemia, prolonged PT/PTT, elevated CPK, and markedly elevated CRP in severe illness
Hemoconcentration from vascular leakage is usually evident (most marked in HFRS and severe dengue)
redFlags: Strict barrier nursing and infection-control isolation with appropriate PPE are mandatory for suspected VHF (except dengue, orthohantavirus, RVFV, or yellow fever); isolate and hospitalize even before clinical signs appear
Immediately notify infectious disease specialists and public health authorities if filovirid disease is suspected on epidemiologic or clinical grounds
Progressive multiorgan dysfunction: shock, acute kidney injury, CNS injury (encephalopathy, coma, seizures), respiratory failure, and severe hemorrhage signal critical illness

Exposure history raising suspicion: caves/mines, direct contact with bats, nonhuman primates, or bushmeat, contact with severely ill local residents, or patient-to-patient/healthcare-worker clusters in rural hospitals
Hemodynamic instability/hypotension and capillary leak with effusions and edema
Pregnancy and labor are associated with severe complications and poor outcomes (clotting-factor consumption, fetal loss, severe peripartum hemorrhage)
harrison.prognosis: FVD is among the most severe acute human viral diseases and generally carries a poor prognosis, though with far more heterogeneity than historically assumed (the long-cited 70-90% case-fatality rate for EVD has required revision). Outcome likely depends on the specific filovirid, host factors (age, immune status, coinfections, host genetics), exposure route and dose, viral load, presence and severity of organ dysfunction, and critically the availability of filovirid-specific countermeasures and supportive/critical care. Even with effective EBOV-specific therapeutics, outcomes in severe EVD with high viral loads and complex organ dysfunction remain suboptimal. For other VHFs prognosis varies widely by agent (e.g., Argentinian/Bolivian hemorrhagic fevers can have case-fatality rates exceeding 50% in individual outbreaks) (pp.1675, 1685-1687).
pitfalls: Filovirid/VHF disease cannot be diagnosed on clinical presentation alone; numerous more common febrile illnesses (especially malaria and typhoid) closely mimic it and are far more likely in non-outbreak settings, so do not anchor on VHF without epidemiologic context and laboratory confirmation.
Absence of overt hemorrhage does not exclude VHF, since hemorrhagic manifestations are often neither the most prominent nor the most severe feature.
Treat DIC only with clear laboratory evidence and feasible monitoring; there is no proven benefit otherwise.

Fluid management is a balancing act: VHF patients are commonly hypovolemic from insensible and GI losses, yet may also have decreased cardiac output, capillary leak, and oliguria requiring judicious fluids and inotropic/vasopressor support.
Do not assume respiratory/aerosol spread for filovirids in natural settings and do not reuse medical equipment (gloves, syringes) used for an infected patient.
harrison.severityClassification: No formal numeric severity score is provided; clinically, the illness progresses from an incubation period through a nonspecific febrile prodrome (early phase) to a peak phase, with severity marked by progressive multiorgan dysfunction (shock, acute kidney injury, respiratory failure, CNS injury, severe hemorrhage). Filovirid disease course is depicted across incubation, early, peak, and recovery phases. Severity and case-fatality vary by causative virus and the availability of specific countermeasures and supportive care (pp.1675, 1683-1686).
